chapters.title: The Last Night
paragraphs: Mr. Utterson was sitting by his fireside one evening after dinner, when he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole.
“Bless me, Poole, what brings you here?” he cried; and then, taking a second look at him, “What ails you?” he added. “Is the doctor ill?”
“Mr. Utterson,” said the man, “there is something wrong.”
“Take a seat, and here is a glass of wine for you,” said the lawyer. “Now, take your time, and tell me plainly what you want.”

“You know the doctor’s ways, sir,” replied Poole, “and how he shuts himself away. Well, he’s shut himself in the study again, and I don’t like it, sir—I’ll be damned if I like it. Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”
“Now, my good man,” said the lawyer, “be explicit. What are you afraid of?”
“I’ve been afraid for about a week,” returned Poole, doggedly ignoring the question, “and I can bear it no more.”

The man’s look bore out his words; his manner had changed for the worse, and except for the moment he’d first announced his fear, he had not once met the lawyer’s eyes. Even now he sat with the glass of wine untouched on his knee, staring at a corner of the floor. “I can bear it no more,” he repeated.
“Come,” said the lawyer, “I see you have some good reason, Poole; I see there is something seriously wrong. Try to tell me what it is.”
“I think there’s been foul play,” said Poole hoarsely.
“Foul play!” cried the lawyer, badly frightened and, as a result, rather inclined to be irritated. “What foul play? What does the man mean?”
“I daren’t say, sir,” was the answer; “but will you come along with me and see for yourself?”

Mr. Utterson’s only answer was to rise and get his hat and overcoat; but he noticed, with wonder, how great the relief was on the butler’s face, and perhaps with no less wonder that the wine was still untouched when he set it down to follow.

It was a wild, cold March night, the kind you’d expect for the season: a pale moon lying on her back as if the wind had tipped her over, and thin, ragged clouds racing past. The wind made talking difficult and stung color into their faces. It seemed, besides, to have swept the streets unusually bare of passersby, for Mr. Utterson thought he had never seen that part of London so empty. He wished it were otherwise; never in his life had he felt so sharp a wish to see and touch his fellow human beings, for however hard he fought it, a crushing sense that something terrible was coming had settled over his mind. When they reached the square, it was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden lashed themselves against the railings. Poole, who had kept a pace or two ahead the whole way, now stopped in the middle of the pavement, and despite the biting cold, took off his hat and mopped his brow with a red handkerchief. But for all the haste of his coming, this was not the sweat of exertion he wiped away—it was the moisture of some choking anguish, for his face was white and his voice, when he spoke, harsh and broken.
“Well, sir,” he said, “here we are, and God grant there be nothing wrong.”
“Amen, Poole,” said the lawyer.
At that the servant knocked in a very cautious manner; the door was opened on the chain; and a voice asked from within, “Is that you, Poole?”
“It’s all right,” said Poole. “Open the door.”

The hall, when they entered it, was brightly lit; the fire was built up high; and around the hearth all the servants, men and women, stood huddled together like a flock of sheep. At the sight of Mr. Utterson, the housemaid broke into hysterical whimpering; and the cook, crying out, “Bless God! it’s Mr. Utterson,” ran forward as if to take him in her arms.
“What, what? Are you all here?” said the lawyer peevishly. “Very irregular, very unseemly; your master would be far from pleased.”
“They’re all afraid,” said Poole.
Blank silence followed, no one protesting; only the maid raised her voice and now wept loudly.

“Hold your tongue!” Poole snapped at her, with a fierceness that betrayed his own frayed nerves; and indeed, when the girl had so suddenly raised the note of her lament, they had all started and turned toward the inner door with faces full of dread. “Now,” the butler went on, turning to the knife-boy, “bring me a candle, and let’s get this over with at once.” Then he asked Mr. Utterson to follow him, and led the way to the back garden.
“Now, sir,” he said, “come as quietly as you can. I want you to hear, and I don’t want you to be heard. And listen, sir—if he should happen to ask you in, don’t go.”

Mr. Utterson’s nerves, at this unexpected turn, gave such a jolt that he nearly lost his balance; but he gathered his courage and followed the butler into the laboratory building, through the surgical theatre with its clutter of crates and bottles, to the foot of the stairs. There Poole motioned him to stand aside and listen, while he himself set down the candle, and, with a visible effort of will, climbed the steps and knocked, somewhat unsteadily, on the red baize of the study door.
“Mr. Utterson, sir, asking to see you,” he called; and even as he said it, he signaled urgently again for the lawyer to listen.
A voice answered from within: “Tell him I cannot see anyone,” it said, in a complaining tone.

“Thank you, sir,” said Poole, with something like triumph in his voice; and taking up his candle, he led Mr. Utterson back across the yard and into the great kitchen, where the fire was out and the beetles were leaping on the floor.
“Sir,” he said, looking Mr. Utterson in the eye, “was that my master’s voice?”
“It seems much changed,” replied the lawyer, very pale, but returning look for look.

“Changed? Well, yes, I think so,” said the butler. “Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be fooled about his voice? No, sir—my master’s been done away with; he was done away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out in God’s name; and who’s in there instead of him, and why it stays there, is a thing that cries out to Heaven, Mr. Utterson!”

“That’s a very strange story, Poole; it’s a wild story, my man,” said Mr. Utterson, biting his finger. “Suppose it were as you suppose—suppose Dr. Jekyll had been, well, murdered—what could make the murderer stay? That doesn’t hold up; it doesn’t stand to reason.”

“Well, Mr. Utterson, you’re a hard man to satisfy, but I’ll manage it yet,” said Poole. “All this last week—you should know—him, or it, whatever it is that lives in that study, has been crying out night and day for some kind of medicine and can’t get it to suit him. It used to be his way—the master’s, I mean—to write his orders on a sheet of paper and throw it out onto the stairs. That’s all we’ve had this week: papers, a shut door, and even his meals left there to be smuggled in when no one was looking. Well, sir, every day—yes, and two or three times some days—there have been orders and complaints, and I’ve been sent flying to every wholesale chemist in town. Every time I brought the stuff back, there’d be another paper telling me to return it because it wasn’t pure, and another order to a different firm. This drug is wanted something terrible, sir, whatever it’s for.”
“Have you any of these papers?” asked Mr. Utterson.

Poole felt in his pocket and handed over a crumpled note, which the lawyer, leaning nearer the candle, examined carefully. It read: “Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw. He assures them that their last sample is impure and quite useless for his present purpose. In the year 18—, Dr. J. purchased a fairly large quantity from Messrs. M. He now asks them to search with the greatest care, and should any of the same quality remain, to send it to him at once. Expense is no consideration. The importance of this to Dr. J. can hardly be overstated.” So far the letter had run calmly enough, but here, with a sudden splutter of the pen, the writer’s feeling had broken loose. “For God’s sake,” he added, “find me some of the old.”
“This is a strange note,” said Mr. Utterson; and then sharply, “How is it you have it open?”
“The man at Maw’s was mighty angry, sir, and he threw it back at me like so much dirt,” returned Poole.
“This is unquestionably the doctor’s handwriting, don’t you think?” the lawyer went on.
“I thought it looked like it,” said the servant, rather sulkily; and then, in a different tone, “But what does handwriting matter?” he said. “I’ve seen him!”
“Seen him?” repeated Mr. Utterson. “Well?”

“That’s it!” said Poole. “It happened like this. I came suddenly into the theatre from the garden. It seems he’d slipped out to look for this drug or whatever it is, because the study door was open, and there he was at the far end of the room, digging among the crates. He looked up when I came in, gave a kind of cry, and bolted upstairs into the study. I saw him for only a minute, but it made the hair stand up on my head like quills. Sir, if that was my master, why was he wearing a mask? If it was my master, why did he cry out like a rat and run from me? I’ve served him long enough. And then…” The man paused and passed his hand over his face.

“These are all very strange circumstances,” said Mr. Utterson, “but I think I’m beginning to see the light. Your master, Poole, is plainly in the grip of one of those diseases that both torture and disfigure the sufferer; that would explain, for all I know, the change in his voice; it would explain the mask and his avoidance of his friends; it would explain his eagerness to find this drug, by means of which the poor soul still hopes for eventual recovery—God grant he isn’t deceived! There’s my explanation; sad enough, Poole, yes, and dreadful to think about, but it’s plain and natural, it holds together, and it spares us from any excessive alarm.”

“Sir,” said the butler, turning a sort of blotchy pale, “that thing was not my master, and that’s the truth. My master”—here he looked around and began to whisper—“is a tall, well-built man, and that one was more of a dwarf.” Utterson tried to protest. “Oh, sir,” cried Poole, “do you think I don’t know my master after twenty years? Do you think I don’t know where his head comes to on the study door, where I saw him every morning of my life? No, sir, that thing in the mask was never Dr. Jekyll—God knows what it was, but it was never Dr. Jekyll; and in my heart I believe there’s been murder done.”

“Poole,” replied the lawyer, “if you say that, it becomes my duty to make certain. Much as I want to spare your master’s feelings, much as I am puzzled by this note which seems to prove he is still alive, I shall consider it my duty to break down that door.”
“Ah, Mr. Utterson, now you’re talking!” cried the butler.
“And now comes the second question,” Utterson went on: “Who is going to do it?”
“Why, you and me, sir,” was the fearless reply.
“Well said,” returned the lawyer; “and whatever comes of it, I shall make it my business to see that you don’t lose by it.”
“There’s an axe in the theatre,” Poole continued; “and you might take the kitchen poker for yourself.”
The lawyer took that crude but heavy tool in his hand and balanced it. “Do you know, Poole,” he said, looking up, “that you and I are about to put ourselves in some danger?”
“You may well say so, sir,” returned the butler.
“Then we’d better be honest with each other,” said the other. “We both think more than we’ve said; let’s speak plainly. This masked figure you saw—did you recognize it?”

“Well, sir, it moved so fast, and the creature was so hunched over, that I could hardly swear to it,” was the answer. “But if you mean, was it Mr. Hyde?—why, yes, I think it was! You see, it was much the same size, and it had the same quick, light way of moving; and besides, who else could have gotten in by the laboratory door? You haven’t forgotten, sir, that at the time of the murder he still had the key with him? But that’s not all. I don’t know, Mr. Utterson, whether you ever met this Mr. Hyde?”
“Yes,” said the lawyer, “I spoke with him once.”

“Then you must know as well as the rest of us that there was something odd about that gentleman—something that gave a man a turn—I don’t rightly know how to put it, sir, except this: that it made you feel cold and thin right down to your marrow.”
“I admit I felt something of what you describe,” said Mr. Utterson.

“Just so, sir,” returned Poole. “Well, when that masked thing jumped like a monkey out from among the chemicals and darted into the study, it went down my spine like ice. Oh, I know it’s not evidence, Mr. Utterson; I’m educated enough to know that; but a man has his feelings, and I give you my word on the Bible that it was Mr. Hyde!”

“Yes, yes,” said the lawyer. “My fears point the same way. I’m afraid evil was built into that connection from the start—evil was bound to come of it. Yes, truly, I believe you; I believe poor Harry has been killed; and I believe his murderer—for what purpose, God alone can tell—is still lurking in his victim’s room. Well, let vengeance be our watchword. Call Bradshaw.”
The footman came at the summons, very pale and nervous.

“Pull yourself together, Bradshaw,” said the lawyer. “This suspense, I know, is wearing on all of you; but we mean to put an end to it now. Poole and I are going to force our way into the study. If everything is all right, my shoulders are broad enough to bear the blame. But meanwhile, in case something really is wrong, or some wrongdoer tries to escape by the back, you and the boy must go round the corner with a pair of good sticks and take your post at the laboratory door. We give you ten minutes to get to your positions.”

As Bradshaw left, the lawyer checked his watch. “And now, Poole, let us get to ours,” he said, and, tucking the poker under his arm, led the way into the yard. Clouds had banked over the moon, and it was now quite dark. The wind, which only reached that deep well of a courtyard in gusts and drafts, tossed the candlelight back and forth about their steps, until they reached the shelter of the theatre, where they sat down in silence to wait. London hummed steadily all around them, but nearer at hand the stillness was broken only by the sound of footsteps pacing back and forth across the study floor.

“So it goes, walking all day, sir,” Poole whispered; “yes, and most of the night too. Only when a new sample comes from the chemist is there any break in it. Ah, it’s a guilty conscience that’s such an enemy to rest! Ah, sir, there’s blood shed foully in every step of it! But listen again, come closer—put your whole heart into your ears, Mr. Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor’s foot?”

The steps fell light and strange, with a certain sway to them, slow as they went; quite different from the heavy, creaking tread of Henry Jekyll. Utterson sighed. “Is there never anything else?” he asked.
Poole nodded. “Once,” he said. “Once I heard it weeping!”
“Weeping? How do you mean?” said the lawyer, feeling a sudden chill of horror.
“Weeping like a woman, or a lost soul,” said the butler. “I came away with that on my heart, so that I could have wept myself.”

But now the ten minutes were nearly up. Poole dug the axe out from under a stack of packing straw; the candle was set on the nearest table to light their attack; and they crept forward, holding their breath, to where that patient foot was still going up and down, up and down, in the stillness of the night.

“Jekyll,” Utterson cried in a loud voice, “I demand to see you.” He paused a moment, but no reply came. “I am warning you fairly, our suspicions are aroused, and I must and will see you,” he went on; “if not by fair means, then by foul—if not with your consent, then by force!”
“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God’s sake, have mercy!”
“Ah, that’s not Jekyll’s voice—it’s Hyde’s!” cried Utterson. “Break down the door, Poole!”

Poole swung the axe over his shoulder; the blow shook the building, and the red baize door lurched against the lock and hinges. A dreadful shriek, like pure animal terror, rang out from the study. Up went the axe again, and again the panels cracked and the frame jumped; four times the blow fell, but the wood was tough and the fittings well made, and it was not until the fifth blow that the lock burst and the wreckage of the door fell inward onto the carpet.

The two men, shaken by the violence they had just done and by the silence that followed, drew back a little and looked in. There lay the study before their eyes in the quiet lamplight: a good fire glowing and crackling on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin note, a drawer or two open, papers neatly arranged on the desk, and, near the fire, things set out for tea—the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glass-fronted cabinets full of chemicals, the most ordinary room in London that night.

Right in the middle lay the body of a man, badly contorted and still twitching. They crept nearer on tiptoe, turned it onto its back, and saw the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes cut to the doctor’s size; the muscles of his face still moved as if with some trace of life, but life itself was quite gone; and by the crushed vial in his hand and the strong smell of kernels hanging in the air, Utterson knew he was looking at the body of a man who had killed himself.
“We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save him or punish him. Hyde has gone to his reckoning; and all that’s left for us now is to find your master’s body.”

The greater part of the building was taken up by the theatre, which filled almost the whole ground floor and was lit from above, and by the study, which formed an upper floor at one end and looked out onto the courtyard. A corridor connected the theatre to the door on the side street, and the study was reached separately by a second flight of stairs. Besides these there were a few dark closets and a large cellar. They now searched all of it thoroughly. Each closet needed only a glance, since all were empty, and all, judging by the dust that fell from their doors, had stood unopened for a long time. The cellar, indeed, was filled with rickety old lumber, mostly left over from the surgeon who had owned the building before Jekyll; but even as they opened its door, a solid mat of cobweb that had sealed the entrance for years came falling down, telling them that further search there would be pointless. Nowhere was there any trace of Henry Jekyll, dead or alive.
Poole stamped on the flagstones of the corridor. “He must be buried here,” he said, listening to the sound.
“Or he may have fled,” said Utterson, and he turned to examine the door on the side street. It was locked, and lying nearby on the flagstones they found the key, already stained with rust.
“This does not look like it has been used,” observed the lawyer.
“Used!” echoed Poole. “Don’t you see, sir, it’s broken—as if someone had stamped on it?”
“Yes,” Utterson went on, “and the broken edges are rusty too.” The two men looked at each other, frightened. “This is beyond me, Poole,” said the lawyer. “Let us go back to the study.”

They climbed the stairs in silence, and, still glancing now and then in awe at the dead body, went on to examine the contents of the study more closely. On one table there were signs of chemical work: several measured heaps of some white salt laid out on glass dishes, as if for an experiment the unfortunate man had never gotten to finish.
“That’s the same drug I was always bringing him,” said Poole; and just as he spoke, the kettle boiled over with a startling noise.

This drew them to the fireside, where the easy chair stood cozily drawn up, and the tea things sat ready at the sitter’s elbow, sugar already in the cup. Several books stood on a shelf; one lay open beside the tea things, and Utterson was astonished to find it a copy of a devout work that Jekyll had more than once praised highly—annotated, in his own hand, with startling blasphemies.

Next, as they went on looking over the room, the searchers came to the tall standing mirror, into whose depths they looked with an involuntary sense of horror. But it was angled so as to show them nothing but the rosy glow playing across the ceiling, the fire sparkling over and over in the glazed fronts of the cabinets, and their own pale, frightened faces bending forward to look in.
“This mirror has seen some strange things, sir,” whispered Poole.

“And surely nothing stranger than itself,” echoed the lawyer in the same low voice. “For what did Jekyll”—he caught himself at the word with a start, then, overcoming the lapse—“what could Jekyll want with it?” he said.
“You may well say that!” said Poole.

Next they turned to the desk. Among the neat stack of papers, a large envelope lay on top, bearing, in the doctor’s hand, the name of Mr. Utterson. The lawyer broke the seal, and several enclosures fell to the floor. The first was a will, drawn up in the same eccentric terms as the one he had returned six months before—meant to serve as a testament in case of death and a deed of gift in case of disappearance—but in place of the name of Edward Hyde, the lawyer, with indescribable astonishment, read the name of Gabriel John Utterson. He looked at Poole, then back at the paper, and finally at the dead man stretched on the carpet.
“My head is spinning,” he said. “He has been in possession of all this for days; he had no reason to like me; he must have raged to see himself replaced; and yet he has not destroyed this document.”

He picked up the next paper; it was a short note in the doctor’s hand, dated at the top. “Oh, Poole!” the lawyer cried, “he was alive and here today. He cannot have been gotten rid of in so short a time—he must still be alive, he must have fled! But then, why flee? And how? And in that case, can we really call this a suicide? Oh, we must be careful. I can see we may yet drag your master into some terrible catastrophe.”
“Why don’t you read it, sir?” asked Poole.
“Because I am afraid to,” replied the lawyer solemnly. “God grant I have no reason to be!” And with that he lifted the paper to his eyes and read as follows:

“My dear Utterson,—By the time this reaches you, I will have disappeared, though under what circumstances I have no way of foreseeing; but my instinct, and everything about my nameless situation, tells me that the end is certain and must come soon. Go, then, and first read the account that Lanyon warned me he was to place in your hands; and if you care to hear more, turn to the confession of
“Your unworthy and unhappy friend,
“HENRY JEKYLL.”
“There was a third enclosure?” asked Utterson.
“Here, sir,” said Poole, and handed him a thick packet, sealed in several places.

The lawyer put it in his pocket. “I will say nothing of this paper. If your master has fled or is dead, we may at least save his reputation. It is now ten; I must go home and read these documents in quiet, but I shall be back before midnight, when we shall send for the police.”

They went out, locking the door of the theatre behind them; and Utterson, once more leaving the servants gathered around the fire in the hall, trudged back to his office to read the two accounts that would now explain this mystery.
